content_html:
Traditional and Roth IRAs share the same contribution limit but tax your money at opposite ends. A traditional IRA may give you a deduction now and taxes withdrawals later. A Roth IRA gives no deduction now, but qualified withdrawals are tax-free. This calculator puts the same yearly contribution into each account and shows which leaves you with more spendable money in retirement, along with the retirement tax rate at which the answer flips.

How to use this calculator

  1. Ages and annual contribution: the amount you would put into either account each year. Tick "Contribute the maximum" to use the 2026 limit for your age.
  2. Tax rate now and in retirement: these two numbers drive most of the result. Use your marginal rate today (federal plus state) and the average rate you expect to pay on withdrawals.
  3. Expected annual return: the same return is used for both accounts.
  4. Invest the traditional IRA tax savings: leave this on for a like-for-like test. A $7,500 Roth contribution costs $7,500 of take-home pay, while a deductible $7,500 traditional contribution costs less because it cuts your tax bill. Investing that saving means both choices use the same amount of your money.
  5. Income and eligibility: enter your filing status, MAGI and workplace plan coverage to see whether the traditional contribution is deductible and whether you can contribute directly to a Roth.
  6. Retirement withdrawals: how many years you will draw the money down and what it earns meanwhile, used to turn each total into a yearly income.

How the comparison works

Both accounts receive the same contributions and earn the same return, so they reach the same balance. The difference is tax:

  • Roth IRA: the whole balance is yours to spend.
  • Traditional IRA: the balance is reduced by your retirement tax rate (non-deductible contributions excepted), then the side account built from your yearly tax savings is added. That side account is an ordinary investment account, so its earnings are taxed every year at your current rate.

The break-even rate is the retirement tax rate at which both totals match. If your expected retirement rate is below it, the traditional IRA comes out ahead; above it, the Roth does. With a 0% return the break-even equals your current rate exactly. With a positive return it sits a little lower, because the side account's earnings are taxed while the IRA's are not.

Worked example

A 30-year-old puts $7,500 a year into an IRA until 65 and earns 6%. Their tax rate is 22% now and is expected to be 15% in retirement. Nobody in the household has a workplace plan, so the traditional contribution is fully deductible.

  • Either account grows to $885,906.
  • The Roth IRA is worth all $885,906 after tax.
  • The traditional IRA owes $132,886 of tax on withdrawal, but the invested tax savings add $146,043, for a total of $899,064. The traditional IRA is ahead by $13,157.
  • The break-even retirement tax rate is about 16.5%.
  • Spread over 25 years at 5%, that's about $59,864 a year from the Roth and $60,753 a year from the traditional IRA.

If the same person expects to pay 22% in retirement too, the traditional IRA drops to $837,050 and the Roth leads by $48,856.

Things the numbers don't capture

  • Future tax law is unknown, which is why some savers split contributions between the two.
  • Traditional IRAs have required minimum distributions; your own Roth IRA does not.
  • Traditional withdrawals raise taxable income, which can affect how much of your Social Security is taxed and Medicare premiums.
  • Roth contributions (not earnings) can be taken out at any time, which adds flexibility.

faq.question: Is a Roth IRA always better for young savers?
faq.answer: Not always, but often. Young savers tend to be in a lower tax bracket now than they will be later, which favors paying tax today with a Roth. If your current rate is high and you expect a lower rate in retirement, the traditional IRA can win.

faq.question: Can I split my contribution between a traditional and a Roth IRA?
faq.answer: Yes. You can divide the $7,500 limit ($8,600 at 50 and over) between the two in any proportion, which spreads your bets on future tax rates.

faq.question: What if I can't deduct a traditional IRA contribution?
faq.answer: Without the deduction, a traditional IRA loses its main advantage: you pay tax now and still pay tax on the earnings later. If you are also within the Roth income limits, a Roth contribution usually comes out ahead in that case.

faq.question: What tax rate should I use for retirement?
faq.answer: Use the average rate you expect on withdrawals, not your top bracket. Many retirees have less income than when working, but large traditional balances, pensions and Social Security can keep the rate higher than expected.

faq.question: Does the comparison include state income tax?
faq.answer: Only if you include it in the tax rates you enter. Add your state rate to the federal rate for both now and retirement, and remember that moving to a state with a different tax rate changes the answer.
